problem: Prior indoor social-navigation planners and outdoor terrain-traversability methods (semantic segmentation, self-supervised) are each built for one perception or navigation task and do not generalize across indoor and outdoor settings. Prior VLM navigation work mostly decides where to go (goal or landmark grounding), not how to move: stay on pavement, use crosswalks, don't cut through groups. Large VLMs are also too slow and too weak at spatial reasoning to be used directly for real-time robot control.
motivation: Humans navigate by recognizing the context they are in (corridor, crowd, terrain, crosswalk) and following explicit and implicit social and terrain rules. VLMs have the zero-shot semantic understanding needed to mimic this. However, VLMs are slow (several seconds per query), unreliable at spatial relations such as distance and relative location, and easily distracted by obstacle regions. So they must be used sparingly, with succinct context-specific prompts, and grounded with geometric sensing.
key_idea: Use CLIP to classify the robot's current context and pick a matching short behavior prompt. Overlay numbered markers only on lidar-verified obstacle-free locations in the RGB image. GPT-4v or Gemini then picks the numbers that satisfy the behavior, and those numbers become a reference path that a DWA planner follows in real time.
insight: The key design choice is a division of labor: lidar and occupancy geometry decide which locations are feasible, the VLM makes only the semantic choice among them, and a classical planner handles real-time collision avoidance. The MMVM ablation (Table I) shows why this matters. Placing markers on obstacles as well raises indoor path error sharply (Scen. 1 GPT-4v: 1.576 vs 0.187), raises unacceptable paths (0.913 vs 0.0), and lengthens inference (4.86 s vs 3.48 s), because VLMs cannot reliably reason about obstacles and spatial layout. Replacing context-based prompting with one long all-scenario prompt gives similar path error, but inference is slower. It also raises unacceptable paths in scenarios with intricate behaviors (Scen. 2 GPT-4v: 0.223 vs 0.167; Scen. 4: 0.166 vs 0.055), so short context-specific prompts make intricate rules easier to follow. The paper claims the full method is best 'in all cases', but this is not strictly true. With Gemini in Scen. 3, the full method's path error (0.979) is worse than without CbP (0.817).
method: Context-based behavior prompt: CLIP scores the RGB image against k=5 prompts of the form 'This is a picture of c_i' (indoor corridor, people, outdoor terrain, crosswalk, etc.). The argmax context selects a short behavior phrase (e.g. 'keep close to the right wall', 'move on pavement'), which is inserted into a fixed template: 'You are navigating a robot... Pick a list of numbers marked in the image such that the robot ___'.

Multi-modal visual marking (MMVM): candidate grids are laid out as l rows × m columns on a 200×200 robot-centric lidar occupancy map, with obstacles inflated by the robot radius (l=2 outdoors, 3 indoors; m=6; d_row=2.5 m; d_col=2 m). A grid is kept only if the line from the robot to it is obstacle-free. Kept grids are projected into the RGB image by homography and numbered left-to-right, row by row.

Large-VLM reference path: the marked image and the behavior prompt are sent to GPT-4v or Gemini (online API), which returns a list of marker numbers. These index back to occupancy-map grids and are transformed into the robot frame as the reference path T_ref.

Reference-path-following DWA: the DWA objective Q1 (heading, obstacle distance, velocity) is augmented with a cost α4·|lateral offset| to the nearest reference point ahead of the robot. This term is active only when the goal direction lies within the camera FOV, so the robot does not stray from the goal.

Extrapolation and re-querying: if the CLIP context is unchanged and the robot is within d_thresh ≈ v_max·t_query (4 m) of the last reference point, the path is linearly extrapolated by d_row. If the extrapolated point is obstacle-free and CLIP labels a 200×200 patch around it as paved, it becomes the next waypoint; otherwise the large VLM is re-queried. This cuts queries by about 50% in constant-context environments.

Hallucination mitigation: a phrase is added to the prompt telling the VLM to treat each query as a new task and ignore past inputs and outputs. This counters repeated patterned outputs such as [1,2,3,4,5] on sequences of similar images.

setting.backbone: GPT-4v or Gemini (frozen, via API) for reference-path selection; CLIP (frozen, local) for context and terrain-patch classification; classical DWA planner for control
setting.observation: monocular RGB (Zed 2i) + 3D lidar (Velodyne VLP16) converted to a 2D robot-centric occupancy grid; goal direction for the planner
setting.action_space: VLM selects numbered free-space markers forming a reference path; DWA outputs continuous (v, ω) velocity commands (v_max = 0.3 m/s)
setting.privileged: none (goal position given to the planner; online lidar occupancy used)

numbers_note: The paper uses no standard embodied-navigation benchmark; all results come from the authors' own real-world scenarios (Scen. 1–4, mapped to indoor corridors, indoor with people, outdoor terrains and outdoor crosswalks following Sec. V-D). The number of trials and episodes is not stated. The Table I column is labeled '% Unacceptable Paths', but values are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.083) and are copied as printed. The benefit of extrapolation (about 50% fewer re-queries) is reported only in text. The detour-sign scenario is qualitative only (Fig. 1), and further results are deferred to a technical report.
results: With GPT-4v, CoNVOI's trajectories are closest to human teleoperation (lowest Fréchet distance) in all four real-world scenarios. It beats Frozone indoors (Scen. 1: 0.521 vs 0.577; Scen. 2: 0.709 vs 0.866) and GA-Nav/PSP-Net/DWA outdoors (Scen. 3: 1.083 vs GA-Nav 1.957; Scen. 4: 0.863 vs PSP-Net 2.068). The costs are longer normalized paths (about 1.19–1.24) and lower mean velocity (0.238–0.289 vs about 0.39–0.49 m/s, capped by v_max = 0.3 m/s). In ablations, removing MMVM raises indoor reference-path error roughly 5–8× and unacceptable paths to 0.79–0.91. Removing context-based prompting increases inference time and unacceptable paths in the crowd and crosswalk scenarios.
limitations: Remote large-VLM latency (about 3.3–6.4 s per query plus network) forces a low max speed (0.3 m/s), makes the method unsuitable for highly dynamic crowds, and occasionally leaves no reference path outdoors, falling back to plain DWA. Coarse marker spacing (d_col) produces wavy trajectories, and finer spacing raises inference time.
The context set and behavior phrases are hand-designed (k=5), and outputs are sensitive to vague prompt wording. The VLM hallucinates patterned outputs when shown sequences of similar images.

Only local egocentric reasoning with no global or top-down information (e.g. cannot find a crosswalk that is out of view). Evaluation is small-scale and real-world only, with no standard benchmark or reported trial counts.
